Homework 4: EM and HMMs

homework4.Rmd
library(STATS230)
library(ggplot2)
library(bench)

Problem 1: Mixture of Normals

We consider a mixture of two normal distributions with unknown means μ1,μ2\mu_1, \mu_2 and known variances σ1=1.0\sigma_1 = 1.0, σ2=0.8\sigma_2 = 0.8. Pairs (x1,y1),…,(xn,yn)(x_1, y_1), \ldots, (x_n, y_n) are i.i.d. with joint distribution

Pr(xi,yi)=[αf(yi,μ1,σ1)]𝟏{xi=1}[(1−α)f(yi,μ2,σ2)]𝟏{xi=2}, \Pr(x_i, y_i) = [\alpha f(y_i, \mu_1, \sigma_1)]^{\mathbf{1}\{x_i = 1\}} [(1 - \alpha) f(y_i, \mu_2, \sigma_2)]^{\mathbf{1}\{x_i = 2\}},

where xi∈{1,2}x_i \in \{1,2\} is a class membership variable that indicates which distribution gave rise to yi∈ℝy_i \in \mathbb{R},

Pr(xi=1)=1−Pr(xi=2)=α, \Pr(x_i = 1) = 1 - \Pr(x_i = 2) = \alpha,

and

f(x,μ,σ)=1σ2πexp(−(x−μ)22σ2). f(x, \mu, \sigma) = \frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left(-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).

We also assume that we observe y=(y1,…,yn)y = (y_1, \ldots, y_n) but do not observe x=(x1,…,xn)x = (x_1, \ldots, x_n). Our goal is to infer α\alpha, μ1\mu_1, and μ2\mu_2 by maximizing the observed data log-likelihood

ℓ(α,μ1,μ2)=∑i=1nln[αf(yi,μ1,σ1)+(1−α)f(yi,μ2,σ2)]. \ell(\alpha, \mu_1, \mu_2) = \sum_{i=1}^n \ln\left[ \alpha f(y_i, \mu_1, \sigma_1) + (1 - \alpha) f(y_i, \mu_2, \sigma_2) \right].

Instead of maximizing the log-likelihood directly, we want to derive an EM algorithm to get MLEs.

(a) Complete log-likelihood

The complete-data likelihood, taking the product over i.i.d. variables, becomes

Pr(x→,y→∣α,μ1,μ2)=∏i=1n[αf(yi∣μ1,σ1)]𝟏{xi=1}[(1−α)f(yi∣μ2,σ2)]𝟏{xi=2}. \Pr(\vec x, \vec y \mid \alpha, \mu_1, \mu_2) = \prod_{i=1}^n \Big[ \alpha f(y_i \mid \mu_1, \sigma_1) \Big]^{\mathbf{1}\{x_i=1\}} \Big[ (1-\alpha) f(y_i \mid \mu_2, \sigma_2) \Big]^{\mathbf{1}\{x_i=2\}}.

Taking logs gives

lnPr(x→,y→∣α,μ1,μ2)=∑i=1n𝟏{xi=1}(lnα+lnf(yi∣μ1,σ1))+𝟏{xi=2}(ln(1−α)+lnf(yi∣μ2,σ2)). \ln\Pr(\vec x, \vec y \mid \alpha, \mu_1, \mu_2) = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{1}\{x_i=1\} \Big( \ln \alpha + \ln f(y_i \mid \mu_1,\sigma_1) \Big) + \mathbf{1}\{x_i=2\} \Big( \ln (1-\alpha) + \ln f(y_i \mid \mu_2,\sigma_2) \Big).

Using lnf(y∣μ,σ)=−ln(σ2π)−(y−μ)22σ2, \ln f(y \mid \mu,\sigma) = -\ln(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}) -\frac{(y-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2},

the complete log-likelihood becomes

lnPr(x→,y→∣α,μ1,μ2)=∑i=1n𝟏{xi=1}[lnα−ln(σ12π)−(yi−μ1)22σ12]+∑i=1n𝟏{xi=2}[ln(1−α)−ln(σ22π)−(yi−μ2)22σ22]. \begin{aligned} \ln\Pr(\vec x, \vec y \mid \alpha, \mu_1, \mu_2) &= \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{1}\{x_i=1\} \left[ \ln\alpha -\ln(\sigma_1\sqrt{2\pi}) -\frac{(y_i-\mu_1)^2}{2\sigma_1^2} \right] \\ &\quad+ \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{1}\{x_i=2\} \left[ \ln(1-\alpha) -\ln(\sigma_2\sqrt{2\pi}) -\frac{(y_i-\mu_2)^2}{2\sigma_2^2} \right]. \end{aligned}

(b) E-step of the EM algorithm

We want to derive an expression for 𝔼[lnPr(x→,y→∣α,μ1,μ2)|y→,α(k),μ1(k),μ2(k)]. \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \ln\Pr(\vec x, \vec y \mid \alpha, \mu_1, \mu_2) \;\middle|\; \vec y, \alpha^{(k)}, \mu_1^{(k)}, \mu_2^{(k)} \right].

Here the expectation is taken with respect to the conditional distribution Pr(x→∣y→,α(k),μ1(k),μ2(k)). \Pr(\vec x \mid \vec y, \alpha^{(k)}, \mu_1^{(k)}, \mu_2^{(k)}). That is, we treat y→\vec y and the current parameter values α(k),μ1(k),μ2(k)\alpha^{(k)}, \mu_1^{(k)}, \mu_2^{(k)} as fixed, and average only over the latent class indicators x→\vec x.

Because the complete log-likelihood is linear in the indicator variables 𝟏{xi=1}\mathbf{1}\{x_i = 1\} and 𝟏{xi=2}\mathbf{1}\{x_i = 2\}, taking expectations simply replaces each indicator with its conditional probability.

Define pi(k)=Pr(xi=1∣yi,α(k),μ1(k),μ2(k)) p_i^{(k)} = \Pr(x_i = 1 \mid y_i, \alpha^{(k)}, \mu_1^{(k)}, \mu_2^{(k)})

For notational convenience. Then we have 𝔼[𝟏{xi=1}∣yi]=pi(k),𝔼[𝟏{xi=2}∣yi]=1−pi(k). \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}\{x_i=1\} \mid y_i] = p_i^{(k)}, \qquad \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}\{x_i=2\} \mid y_i] = 1 - p_i^{(k)}.

Therefore the expected complete log-likelihood becomes 𝔼[lnPr(x→,y→∣α,μ1,μ2)∣y→,α(k),μ1(k),μ2(k)]=∑i=1npi(k)[lnα−ln(σ12π)−(yi−μ1)22σ12]+∑i=1n(1−pi(k))[ln(1−α)−ln(σ22π)−(yi−μ2)22σ22]. \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}\left[\ln\Pr(\vec x, \vec y \mid \alpha, \mu_1, \mu_2) \mid \vec y, \alpha^{(k)}, \mu_1^{(k)}, \mu_2^{(k)}\right] &= \sum_{i=1}^n p_i^{(k)} \left[ \ln\alpha -\ln(\sigma_1\sqrt{2\pi}) -\frac{(y_i-\mu_1)^2}{2\sigma_1^2} \right] \\ &\quad+ \sum_{i=1}^n (1-p_i^{(k)}) \left[ \ln(1-\alpha) -\ln(\sigma_2\sqrt{2\pi}) -\frac{(y_i-\mu_2)^2}{2\sigma_2^2} \right]. \end{aligned}

The important idea is that the only randomness in the complete-data log-likelihood comes from the unobserved labels xix_i. The idea behind EM here is to replace unknown class labels with their current probabilities, then maximize a weighted log-likelihood to get new parameter estimates, and repeat until convergence.

(c) M-step of the EM algorithm

To maximize, we take partial derivatives with respect to α\alpha, μ1\mu_1, and μ2\mu_2.

With respect to α\alpha, we have ∂∂α𝔼[lnPr(x→,y→∣α,μ1,μ2)∣y→,α(k),μ1(k),μ2(k)]=∑i=1npi(k)α−∑i=1n1−pi(k)1−α=0. \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} \mathbb{E}\left[\ln\Pr(\vec x, \vec y \mid \alpha, \mu_1, \mu_2) \mid \vec y, \alpha^{(k)}, \mu_1^{(k)}, \mu_2^{(k)}\right] = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{p_i^{(k)}}{\alpha} - \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1-p_i^{(k)}}{1-\alpha} = 0.

Solving for α\alpha, we get α(k+1)=∑i=1npi(k)n. \alpha^{(k+1)} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n p_i^{(k)}}{n}.

Checking the second derivative, we have ∂2∂α2=−∑i=1npi(k)α2−∑i=1n1−pi(k)(1−α)2<0, \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \alpha^2} = -\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{p_i^{(k)}}{\alpha^2} - \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1-p_i^{(k)}}{(1-\alpha)^2} < 0, so the critical point is a maximum.

With respect to μ1\mu_1, we have ∂∂μ1𝔼[lnPr(x→,y→∣α,μ1,μ2)∣y→,α(k),μ1(k),μ2(k)]=−∑i=1npi(k)(yi−μ1)σ12=0. \frac{\partial}{\partial \mu_1} \mathbb{E}\left[\ln\Pr(\vec x, \vec y \mid \alpha, \mu_1, \mu_2) \mid \vec y, \alpha^{(k)}, \mu_1^{(k)}, \mu_2^{(k)}\right] = -\sum_{i=1}^n p_i^{(k)} \frac{(y_i - \mu_1)}{\sigma_1^2} = 0.

Solving for μ1\mu_1, we get μ1(k+1)=∑i=1npi(k)yi∑i=1npi(k). \mu_1^{(k+1)} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n p_i^{(k)} y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n p_i^{(k)}}.

Checking the second derivative, we have ∂2∂μ12=−∑i=1npi(k)σ12<0, \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \mu_1^2} = -\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{p_i^{(k)}}{\sigma_1^2} < 0, so the critical point is a maximum.

With respect to μ2\mu_2, we have ∂∂μ2𝔼[lnPr(x→,y→∣α,μ1,μ2)∣y→,α(k),μ1(k),μ2(k)]=−∑i=1n(1−pi(k))(yi−μ2)σ22=0. \frac{\partial}{\partial \mu_2} \mathbb{E}\left[\ln\Pr(\vec x, \vec y \mid \alpha, \mu_1, \mu_2) \mid \vec y, \alpha^{(k)}, \mu_1^{(k)}, \mu_2^{(k)}\right] = -\sum_{i=1}^n (1-p_i^{(k)}) \frac{(y_i - \mu_2)}{\sigma_2^2} = 0.

Solving for μ2\mu_2, we get μ2(k+1)=∑i=1n(1−pi(k))yi∑i=1n(1−pi(k)). \mu_2^{(k+1)} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (1-p_i^{(k)}) y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (1-p_i^{(k)})}.

Checking the second derivative, we have ∂2∂μ22=−∑i=1n1−pi(k)σ22<0, \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \mu_2^2} = -\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1-p_i^{(k)}}{\sigma_2^2} <0, so the critical point is a maximum.

Therefore, the EM algorithm is given by the following updates: pi(k)=Pr(xi=1∣yi,α(k),μ1(k),μ2(k))=α(k)f(yi∣μ1(k),σ1)α(k)f(yi∣μ1(k),σ1)+(1−α(k))f(yi∣μ2(k),σ2),i=1,…,n,α(k+1)=∑i=1npi(k)n,μ1(k+1)=∑i=1npi(k)yi∑i=1npi(k),μ2(k+1)=∑i=1n(1−pi(k))yi∑i=1n(1−pi(k)). \begin{aligned} p_i^{(k)} &= \Pr(x_i = 1 \mid y_i, \alpha^{(k)}, \mu_1^{(k)}, \mu_2^{(k)}) \\ &= \frac{\alpha^{(k)} f(y_i \mid \mu_1^{(k)}, \sigma_1)}{\alpha^{(k)} f(y_i \mid \mu_1^{(k)}, \sigma_1) + (1-\alpha^{(k))} f(y_i \mid \mu_2^{(k)}, \sigma_2)}, \ \qquad i = 1, \ldots, n, \\ \alpha^{(k+1)} &= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n p_i^{(k)}}{n}, \\ \mu_1^{(k+1)} &= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n p_i^{(k)} y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n p_i^{(k)}}, \\ \mu_2^{(k+1)} &= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (1-p_i^{(k)}) y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (1-p_i^{(k)})}. \end{aligned}

(d) Implementation and example using mixture_data.txt

The EM algorithm is implemented in the function em_mixture_normals(). The function takes as input a vector of observations y, initial parameter values alpha_init, mu1_init, and mu2_init, and a maximum number of iterations max_iter. The function returns a list containing the final parameter estimates and the log-likelihood at each iteration.

y <- as.vector(read.table(system.file("mixture_data.txt",
                                      package = "STATS230")))[[1]]
rslt <- em_mixture_normals(y)
print(rslt)
#> $alpha
#> [1] 0.3002875
#> 
#> $mu1
#> [1] 1.903574
#> 
#> $mu2
#> [1] 6.027247
#> 
#> $loglik
#>  [1] -575.5030 -567.0335 -566.2514 -566.1876 -566.1826 -566.1822 -566.1822
#>  [8] -566.1822 -566.1822 -566.1822 -566.1822 -566.1822 -566.1822 -566.1822
#> [15] -566.1822 -566.1822
#> 
#> $converged
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $iterations

(e) Simulation study

Now, we will test the performance of our EM algorithm by simulating data from a known mixture of normals and checking if we can recover the true parameters.

set.seed(123)

# True parameters
alpha_true <- 0.3
mu1_true <- 2.1
mu2_true <- 5.2
sigma1 <- 1
sigma2 <- 0.8
datasets <- 100
n_obs <- 300

results_list <- vector("list", length = datasets)
for (d in 1:datasets) {
  # Simulate data
  x <- rbinom(n_obs, size = 1, prob = 1 - alpha_true) + 1  # x_i = 1 or 2
  y <- ifelse(x == 1,
              rnorm(n_obs, mean = mu1_true, sd = sigma1),
              rnorm(n_obs, mean = mu2_true, sd = sigma2))

  # Run EM algorithm on simulated data
  rslt_sim <- em_mixture_normals(y,
                                 mu1_init = quantile(y, 0.25),
                                 mu2_init = quantile(y, 0.75),
                                 sigma1 = sigma1, sigma2 = sigma2)

  # Store results
  results_list[[d]] <- list(
    alpha = rslt_sim$alpha,
    mu1 = rslt_sim$mu1,
    mu2 = rslt_sim$mu2
  )
}

Now, we plot the results from above:

Notice that, above, we initialized the EM algorithm with the 25th and 75th percentiles of the data for mu1_init and mu2_init, respectively. Let’s see how the results change if we do the opposite:

# Run EM algorithm with reversed initializations
results_list_reversed <- vector("list", length = datasets)
for (d in 1:datasets) {
  # Simulate data
  x <- rbinom(n_obs, size = 1, prob = 1 - alpha_true) + 1  # x_i = 1 or 2
  y <- ifelse(x == 1,
              rnorm(n_obs, mean = mu1_true, sd = sigma1),
              rnorm(n_obs, mean = mu2_true, sd = sigma2))
  # Run EM algorithm on simulated data with reversed initializations
  rslt_sim <- em_mixture_normals(y,
                                 mu1_init = quantile(y, 0.75),
                                 mu2_init = quantile(y, 0.25),
                                 sigma1 = sigma1, sigma2 = sigma2)
  # Store results
  results_list_reversed[[d]] <- list(
    alpha = rslt_sim$alpha,
    mu1 = rslt_sim$mu1,
    mu2 = rslt_sim$mu2
  )
}

Now, everything’s reversed! This is known as the “label switching” problem because the likelihood is symmetric in μ1\mu_1 and μ2\mu_2, so the EM algorithm can converge to either mode depending on the initialization. To fix this issue, we can enforce a consistent labeling convention, such as always labeling the component with the smaller mean as component 1. This way, we will always have μ1<μ2\mu_1 < \mu_2, and the algorithm will converge to the same mode regardless of initialization.

Going back to our original results, the question asked for the bias of α̂\hat \alpha and its associated Monte Carlo error:

#> Bias of alpha: 0.002112956
#> Monte Carlo error of alpha: 0.003439607

The bias is small relative to α\alpha, and the Monte Carlo error is larger than the bias, suggesting that the estimator is unbiased.

Problem 2: Hidden Markov Model (Occasionally Dishonest Casino)

The setup of this question is that we are at a casino that sometimes uses a fair die, and sometimes uses a loaded die, and they randomly switch between the two. Initially, the casino selects one of the dice uniformly randomly (i.e., with 1/2 probability for each). We are given the transition probabilities between the two states (1 = fair die, 2 = loaded die) and the probabilities of observing each outcome (1-6) given the state.

(a) Simulating the Casino

The function occasionally_dishonest_casino() simulates a sequence of die rolls from the casino. It takes as input the number of rolls to simulate and returns a list containing the sequence of states (which die was used) and the sequence of observed outcomes.

set.seed(123)

hmm_sim <- occasionally_dishonest_casino(n_obs = 100)

# plot the sequence of states and outcomes
state_outcome_df <- data.frame(
  Time = seq_along(hmm_sim$states),
  State = factor(hmm_sim$states, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Fair", "Loaded")),
  Outcome = hmm_sim$observations
)

ggplot(state_outcome_df, aes(x = Time)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = as.numeric(State)), color = "blue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = Outcome), color = "red", alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "State (1=Fair, 2=Loaded)",
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~ ., name = "Outcome (1-6)")
  ) +
  labs(title = "Simulated Sequence of States and Outcomes") +
  theme_minimal()

(b) Implement Forward and Backward Algorithms

The forward algorithm computes the probability of observing the sequence of outcomes up to time tt and being in state jj at time tt. The backward algorithm computes the probability of observing the sequence of outcomes from time t+1t+1 to the end given that we are in state jj at time tt. Together, these algorithms allow us to compute the probabilities of being in each state at each time point given the entire sequence of observations. The function forward_backward_casino() implements these algorithms. It takes as input the sequence of observations, the initial distribution over states, the transition probabilities, and the emission probabilities, and returns a list containing the forward probabilities (alpha), backward probabilities (beta), and the transition and emission matrices. This function is called internally by occasionally_dishonest_casino() to compute the forward and backward probabilities for the simulated data.

Below, we plot the true state, overlaid with the probability of being in the loaded state at each time point.

state_prob_df <- data.frame(
  Time = seq_along(hmm_sim$states),
  TrueState = hmm_sim$states - 1,
  ProbLoaded = hmm_sim$gamma[, 2]  # Probability of being in the loaded state
)

ggplot(state_prob_df, aes(x = Time)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ProbLoaded), color = "red") +
  geom_line(aes(y = as.numeric(TrueState)), color = "blue") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Probability of Loaded State",
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~ ., name = "True State is Loaded (Indicator)")
  ) +
  labs(title = "Probability of Loaded State Over Time") +
  theme_minimal()
